record.paper_title: Chapter 15: Open Questions and Future Directions in Titan Science
record.context_brief: Timing of fluvial channels and low-latitude seas
record.original_question: When were Titan's low-latitude river channels carved and its low-latitude methane seas filled or drained, and what combination of topography, methane loss, shoreline monitoring, humidity measurements, climate modeling, and fluvial-erosion timescales can reconstruct Titan's drying history?

evidence.quote: 12) When were the river channels carved and the low latitude seas filled?

A consensus is now emerging that Titan appears to be drying out over time, with formerly extensive low-latitude oceans of methane retreating polewards (Larsson and McKay, 2013). However it is important to know the timescale in which this has occurred, since it has important implications for our understanding of Titan’s past history, and the unique nature of its atmosphere.

Given present-day rates of methane loss coupled with Titan’s known topography, the equatorial seas are predicted to have been connected to polar seas 300 Myr ago, and a global ocean to have existed 600 Myr ago (Larsson and McKay, 2013). However, studies of river erosive timescales to form present topography are much less constraining, with estimates ranging from 60 Kyr to 470 Myr (Cartwright et al., 2011).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Titan, the largest moon of Saturn, hosts a methane-based hydrologic cycle: liquid hydrocarbons (primarily methane and ethane) carve fluvial channels, fill polar seas, and exchange with an atmospheric reservoir through evaporation, photochemical loss, and precipitation. Observations indicate that Titan is drying out over geologic time, with formerly extensive low-latitude oceans of methane retreating poleward.

Determine the following:

1. The absolute geologic time at which Titan's low-latitude (equatorial) river channels were carved into the present surface topography.

2. The absolute geologic time at which Titan's low-latitude methane seas were filled, and the time at which they were subsequently drained.

3. A self-consistent reconstruction of Titan's "drying history" — i.e., the time evolution of the global distribution and total inventory of surface liquid methane — that simultaneously fits:
   (a) the present-day topography of equatorial basins and polar basins,
   (b) the present-day rate of atmospheric and photochemical methane loss,
   (c) shoreline-recession measurements at the existing polar seas,
   (d) measurements of near-surface humidity and methane mole fraction,
   (e) general circulation / climate model outputs for past atmospheric states with differing methane abundances, and
   (f) fluvial-erosion timescale estimates needed to incise the observed channel networks to their current depths.

Provide quantitative timescales (with uncertainties) for the filling and draining of equatorial seas, the carving of equatorial fluvial channels, and the transition from a putative global or hemispheric ocean state to the present polar-restricted distribution of liquids.
artifact.category_tag: Planetary science: Titan hydrology and climate evolution
artifact.status_search_result: The question remains open. Published estimates span very wide ranges: methane-loss models predict that equatorial seas would have been connected to polar seas roughly 300 Myr ago and a global methane ocean ~600 Myr ago, while fluvial denudation timescales for forming present equatorial channels range from ~60 kyr to ~470 Myr depending on model inputs. Alternative scenarios invoke episodic methane outbursts a few hundred Myr ago. No consensus reconstruction has been established.

status_evidence.title: Timescale for oceans in the past of Titan (Larsson & McKay, 2013)
status_evidence.snippet: Equatorial seas connected to polar seas ~300 Myr ago; global ocean ~600 Myr ago based on present methane loss rate and topography.
status_evidence.claim: Methane-loss/topography models give 300–600 Myr timescales for prior low-latitude ocean states, but only as model predictions.

status_evidence.title: Channel morphometry, sediment transport, and surficial ages of Titan basins (Cartwright et al., 2011)
status_evidence.snippet: Denudation timescales range from approximately 60 kyr to 470 Myr depending on model inputs.
status_evidence.claim: Fluvial-erosion age estimates for Titan's channels span four orders of magnitude, indicating the timing is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Rivers, Lakes, Dunes, and Rain: Crustal Processes in Titan's Methane Cycle
status_evidence.snippet: Erosional features may be relatively recent and periodically renewed as climate cycles between dry and wet periods.
status_evidence.claim: Review-level synthesis indicates the timing of channel carving and sea filling/draining remains an open problem.
